newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin puts defence ministry in civilian hands.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin puts defence ministry in civilian hands.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin on Wednesday told Defence Minister Igor Rodionov to quit the armed forces and become Russia's first civilian defence minister in more than 70 years.

A presidential order released by the Kremlin said Rodionov, an army general who turned 60 on December 1, would leave the military because of his age, but Yeltsin later explained that he was also launching a new tradition.
The president told Russian news agencies that the defence ministry would in future be headed by a civilian.

"The experience of democratic states testifies that a civilian standing at the helm of the ministry of defence can successfully tackle the whole set of problems of strengthening the state's defence potential and ensuring the vital activity of the army and navy," Yeltsin told Interfax and RIA news agencies.
Rodionov would "continue to resolve the most complicated questions of reforming the armed forces and strengthening the army and the navy", Interfax said, quoting Yeltsin.
Rodionov was named defence minister in July this year after Yeltsin sacked the hawkish and unpopular Pavel Grachev.
He is respected in the armed forces and has been consolidating his grip over Russia's top brass to push ahead with military reform, including the planned creation of a professional army.
Yuri Baturin, secretary of the Defence Council, said the change would give Rodionov more room for manoeuvre.

"Without harming the authority as minister which he had up to the day of the signing of the president's decree, it significantly increases Igor Nikolayevich Rodionov's political opportunities," Baturin told a news conference.

Under reforms outlined in the Russian media and favoured by the West, a civilian defence minister would be responsible for broad policy decisions and a military-run general staff would have direct control of all the armed forces.
Baturin said that whereas now the chief of staff coordinated the activities of army and navy, the council had decided that in future it should take on all branches of the military.
The aim is to end the divisions which have contributed to the low morale in the military and its humiliation in more than 20 months of fighting in the rebel region of Chechnya.
Baturin said it would take time to implement. "Many preparatory steps must be taken...but we will get to this."
He said urgent attention would also be paid next year to a mobilisation plan for the armed forces, where morale is low and many soldiers have not been paid for months.

The military was able to recruit only 13 percent of conscripts on the list for the autumn call-up, he said, and only 30 percent of the military's weapons are up-to-date, as opposed to 60 or 70 percent in leading western countries.
Wednesday's Kommersant Daily newspaper said Rodionov's retirement from the military would be a useful intermediary step towards civilian control.

"Rodionov is "one of us" to the military and the army will gradually get used to taking orders from a man without epaulettes," it said. "This saves the president from the danger that the army might not take to civilian rule."
The last attempt by Russia to put the military under civilian control, in 1917, was unable to stop the army disintegrating in the run-up to the 1918 Bolshevik revolution.

But Pavel Felgenhauer, military specialist at the Sevodnya daily, said Rodionov was not the kind of professional the ministry needed to adapt the military to a market economy. "I do not think that this move will change anything," he said.
